title: El Gran Mariscal: Cumaná to Berruecos, the Keystone of the Libertador Constellation
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Cumaná, birth into the house of Sucre y Alcalá
stops.campa: Antonio José de Sucre is born on 3 February in Cumaná, the ancient port of the eastern coast, fifth child of Colonel Vicente de Sucre y Urbaneja and María Manuela de Alcalá. The family traces itself to Flemish nobility, planted in the New World two centuries before by Charles de Sucre. He is orphaned of his mother before he is seven; his aunt María de Alcalá takes the boy into the little school she has founded, and the port that will one day watch Humboldt step ashore first watches this quieter arrival.
suggested_refs: The Casa Sucre-Alcalá in Cumaná, preserved as a museum to his childhood
sources: turismosucre.com.ve, biografía de Antonio José de Sucre

stops.name: Caracas, the school of Colonel Tomás Mires
stops.campa: Sent from Cumaná to the capital, the boy enters the School of Engineers kept by the Spanish colonel Tomás Mires, and for years bends over mathematics, land-surveying, fortification, and artillery. It is a soldier's geometry he is given here, the measuring of ditches and glacis and the fall of shot, and it will outlast every uniform he wears: the same hand that plots a bastion will one day plot the ground of Ayacucho and read a battlefield like a drawn plan before the guns speak.
suggested_refs: The colonial engineering-school tradition of Caracas under the last Captaincy-General
sources: el-carabobeno.com, 'Sucre, precursor de la ingeniería militar en Venezuela'

stops.name: Cumaná, cadet of the Junta, the fifteen-year-old subteniente
stops.campa: News of the nineteenth of April reaches the east: Caracas has deposed its captain-general and formed a Junta. Vicente de Sucre helps raise the Junta and the militia of Cumaná, and his son marches home to serve it. On 12 July, a boy of fifteen, Antonio José is commissioned subteniente of the Regulated Militia of the Army of the East, in the Company of Noble Hussars of Ferdinand VII: a king's title on a revolution's first commission, the contradiction of every 1810 in the Americas.
suggested_refs: The Junta Suprema de Cumaná, 27 April 1810
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, 'Sucre, Antonio José de'

segments.name: The Eastern Campaigns and the Years of Exile

stops.name: Caracas, the staff of General Miranda
stops.campa: Called up when the war begins in earnest, the young engineer joins the General Staff of Francisco de Miranda, Generalissimo of the First Republic, and is promoted teniente for his conduct under fire. It is a brief apprenticeship: the earthquake of March, the royalist advance from Coro, the Republic already dying on its feet, but it puts him, at seventeen, in the room where the war of independence is first drawn as a war, not a proclamation.
suggested_refs: The First Republic of Venezuela, 1811-1812, and its General Staff under Miranda
sources: redhistoria.com, 'Sucre, el militar que liberó Bolivia'

stops.name: Trinidad, the first exile
stops.campa: Miranda capitulates in July and the First Republic falls; the boy-lieutenant flees across the Gulf of Paria to the British island of Trinidad, one exile among hundreds. Here, among the refugees of a failed revolution, he meets Santiago Mariño, a young officer of means already gathering men and boats for a second attempt. Sucre attaches himself to Mariño's fortune. Trinidad will keep this office for the family of the revolution for another five years: a waiting-room the ocean has set just outside Spain's reach.
suggested_refs: Port of Spain, Trinidad, refuge of the Venezuelan emigrés after 1812
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, 'Sucre, Antonio José de'

stops.name: Güiria, the landing of the Fifty, the Second Republic's war
stops.campa: In January Mariño lands at Güiria with a company scarcely fifty strong, the seed of the whole liberation of the East, and Sucre lands with him, an engineer among improvised soldiers. Within months Mariño's little army has swept the Spanish from Cumaná and Barcelona while, unknown to them at first, Bolívar does the same in the west with his Admirable Campaign. Two republics of the same revolution rise on either side of the country, and Sucre, promoted teniente coronel for his valor, rides with the eastern one toward Caracas.
suggested_refs: Santiago Mariño's 1813 campaign of the East, 'la Reconquista de Oriente'
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, 'Sucre, Antonio José de'

stops.name: Urica, the Second Republic breaks
stops.campa: The Second Republic is already dying under the llanero horror of José Tomás Boves when Sucre's column meets the royalist host at Urica. Boves falls in the melee, run through by a lance, and for a moment the field seems the patriots'. But the army that killed him is itself broken by the day's end, and there is no republic left behind the lines to receive a victory. Sucre, defeated twice in a year at Aragua and now here, flees east with the wreck of Mariño's army, the second attempt at independence ash behind him.
suggested_refs: The death of José Tomás Boves at Urica, 5 December 1814

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the last republican wall
stops.campa: With the mainland lost again, Sucre crosses to New Granada and throws himself into the defense of Cartagena de Indias, walled queen of the Caribbean, besieged that year by the great reconquering armada of Pablo Morillo. He serves the siege through its worst months: hunger inside the walls answering cannon outside them, until the city capitulates in December and the defenders scatter by sea, up the rivers, into the Guayana interior. Twice now the war has ended under him and not killed him; he goes to find where it still lives.
suggested_refs: The siege of Cartagena de Indias, 1815, and Morillo's reconquest fleet
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, 'Sucre, Antonio José de'

stops.name: Angostura, Governor of Guayana, commander of the Lower Orinoco
stops.campa: The war has found new ground on the wide river: Bolívar and Piar have taken Angostura and made the Orinoco basin the free country's spine. On 17 September the Liberator names Sucre Governor of Old Guayana and general commander of the Lower Orinoco, and three weeks later chief of staff of the Cumaná division under Bermúdez. It is administration now as much as combat: provisioning a river-borne republic, and it is the post from which the engineer becomes, in Bolívar's eyes, indispensable.
suggested_refs: Angostura (today Ciudad Bolívar), capital of the Third Republic on the Orinoco
sources: Fundación Empresas Polar, 'Sucre, Antonio José de'
Archivo del Libertador, documentos de Angostura, 1817

stops.name: Angostura, brigadier general, the Congress in session
stops.campa: Bolívar's dream is taking paper form: a Congress sits at Angostura to found a great republic on the model of the north, and while Bolívar rides west toward New Granada and the Andes, Sucre stays close to headquarters, the officer the Liberator trusts with what he cannot watch himself. In August the vice-president Zea promotes him brigadier general; Bolívar ratifies the rank the following February. Those who serve beside him at Angostura begin to call him, without irony, the best-tempered sword in the army.
suggested_refs: The Congress of Angostura, 1819, and the founding charter of Colombia
sources: hazteverecuador.com, 'Antonio José de Sucre, el Gran Mariscal de Ayacucho'
Fundación Empresas Polar, 'Sucre, Antonio José de'

stops.name: Trujillo, the armistice and the regularization of the war
stops.campa: Named Colombia's delegate to treat with Morillo's Spain, Sucre sits at the table in Trujillo and puts his engineer's precision to a different problem: how a ten-year war of extermination might be made, at least, a war between soldiers. The Treaty of Regularization abolishes the war without quarter that has killed as many by the knife as the musket; a six-month armistice follows it. Days later, at nearby Santa Ana, Bolívar and Morillo embrace before both armies: the last civil gesture the two crowns of this war will exchange.
stops.quote: Este tratado es digno del alma del general Sucre: la benignidad, la clemencia, el genio de la beneficencia lo dictaron; él será eterno como el más bello monumento de la piedad aplicada a la guerra.
stops.quote_source: Simón Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre (1825), on the Treaty of Regularization Sucre negotiated at Trujillo
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Regularization of War, Trujillo, 25-26 November 1820
The embrace of Bolívar and Morillo at Santa Ana, 27 November 1820
sources: Archivo del Libertador, tratados de Trujillo, 1820

stops.name: Guayaquil, command of the Army of the South
stops.campa: Guayaquil declared itself free of Spain the previous October and now begs Colombia for a general; Bolívar sends Sucre. He lands to find a port bristling with private ambitions and a scratch army of guayaquileños, and sets at once to making of both a single instrument, the Army of the South, with which to open the road to Quito, still held for the King by President Aymerich in the mountains above.
suggested_refs: The Junta de Gobierno of Guayaquil, independent since 9 October 1820

stops.name: Yaguachi, the first victory of the sierra road
stops.campa: On the approach to the highlands Sucre's column meets and breaks a royalist force at Yaguachi, the first clean patriot victory of the southern campaign. It is a small field by the standards of the war, but it opens the road inland and buys the young general, new to independent command, new to this theatre entirely, the confidence of men who did not yet know if the Colombian sent to lead them could actually win.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Yaguachi, 19 August 1821

stops.name: Huachi, the second battle, and the wound
stops.campa: Pursuing too far past Yaguachi, the patriot vanguard is caught and enveloped by royalist cavalry and infantry at Huachi, near Ambato; the army breaks in disorder, Sucre himself is wounded, and what remains of the Army of the South limps back to Guayaquil with its supplies and half its strength left on the field. It is the low point of the whole southern war: the general's first defeat in independent command, and it teaches him, hard, the difference between a victory and a rout.
suggested_refs: The Second Battle of Huachi, 12 September 1821

stops.name: Guayaquil, the armistice with Aymerich
stops.campa: Beaten but not broken, Sucre buys with diplomacy what he could not yet win with arms: an armistice with President Aymerich that stills the fighting through the end of the year. Behind the truce he rebuilds: recruiting guayaquileños, negotiating for reinforcement from Colombia and from San Martín's Peru, drilling the survivors of Huachi into a real army. The pause he wins here is the whole difference between the general who lost at Huachi and the one who will win at Pichincha.
suggested_refs: The armistice of 19 November 1821 between Sucre and Aymerich
sources: arrecaballo.es, 'Campaña de Sucre en Ecuador 1821. Segunda batalla de Huachi'

stops.name: Riobamba, the road to Quito reopened
stops.campa: With the armistice expired and Colombian reinforcements under Córdova arrived at last, Sucre marches on the highland towns and wins the field at Riobamba, on the plain of Tapi, scattering the royalist cavalry that had ruled the sierra since Huachi. The road to Quito, closed to him for seven months, lies open. Local legend gives the day a heroine as well as a general: Manuela Cañizares and the women of Quito, already conspiring, take Riobamba's news as their signal.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Riobamba (Tapi), 21 April 1822
sources: Enciclopedia del Ecuador, 'Antonio José de Sucre'

stops.name: Pichincha, the volcano's flank, Quito's freedom
stops.campa: By night the patriot columns climb the shoulder of the volcano above Quito, dragging guns up goat-paths in the cold; by eight in the morning Sucre's men hold the heights, and by noon the royalist army of Aymerich is broken below them. The boy-officer Abdón Calderón, shot four times, refuses to leave the line until a fifth wound fells him. Sucre notes his name for the government's gratitude, certain he will not live to receive it. The city that watched the battle from its rooftops is, by evening, free.
stops.quote: Hago una particular memoria de la conducta del teniente Calderón, que habiendo recibido sucesivamente cuatro heridas, no quiso retirarse del combate. Probablemente morirá, pero el Gobierno de la República deberá compensar a su familia los servicios de este oficial heroico.
stops.quote_source: Sucre, official report on the Battle of Pichincha, 28 May 1822
suggested_refs: The Battle of Pichincha, 24 May 1822
Abdón Calderón, the wounded ensign of the report
sources: eluniverso.com, 'Batalla de Pichincha: la estrategia de Sucre'

stops.name: Quito, the capitulation and the entry
stops.campa: The morning after the battle Aymerich signs the capitulation of Quito to the brigadier general of the Colombian army; the royal audiencia of three centuries ends in a single signature. Sucre enters the freed city at twenty-seven years old, a captain-general's fortune won on a mountainside in a single day. Weeks later, on 16 June, Bolívar himself arrives under arches and a rain of flowers to a wound of a different kind: the crown thrown from a balcony, and Manuela Sáenz's black eyes meeting his.
suggested_refs: The Capitulation of Quito, 25 May 1822
sources: bolivar.journey.json (Bolívar's entry into Quito, 16 June 1822, shared theatre)

stops.name: Guayaquil, the port drawn into Colombia
stops.campa: The freedom of Quito leaves unsettled the fate of Guayaquil, whose junta had hoped for its own republic or union with San Martín's Peru. Sucre, acting on Bolívar's instructions and his own authority as military governor, incorporates the port into Colombia days before the Liberator's own arrival: a fait accompli that will color, two weeks later, the closed-door meeting of Bolívar and San Martín in this same city and, some say, tip a continent's balance of glory toward the man from Caracas.
suggested_refs: The Guayaquil Conference of Bolívar and San Martín, 26-27 July 1822

segments.name: Peru, the Sierra Campaign and Ayacucho

stops.name: Lima, sent ahead into the chaos of Peru
stops.campa: Peru's own liberation is unraveling in factional coups: Riva Agüero against the Congress, the Congress against itself, while the royalists still hold the sierra and the south. Bolívar sends Sucre ahead as Colombia's plenipotentiary to hold together what he can; Sucre organizes the wreck of the campaign of the Intermedios, loses ground in the south to a resurgent royalist army, and holds Lima's door until the Liberator himself can cross the Andes in force.
suggested_refs: The Peruvian political crisis of 1823 and the campaign of the Intermedios
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)

stops.name: Huamanga, the army given into his hands
stops.campa: After Junín's silent, saber-only rout of the royalist horse in August, a jealous Congress in Bogotá recalls Bolívar from the army; the Liberator returns to Lima and hands the whole campaign, the last campaign of the mainland war, to Sucre. Through November the patriot column climbs into the cold sierra above Huamanga, shadowing the retreating army of Viceroy La Serna and General Canterac, closing the distance day by day toward the plain the two armies will finally have to share.
stops.quote: La batalla de Ayacucho es la cumbre de la gloria americana, y la obra del general Sucre. La disposición de ella ha sido perfecta, y su ejecución divina.
stops.quote_source: Simón Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre (1825), on the campaign he entrusted to Sucre
suggested_refs: The march from Junín to Ayacucho, November-December 1824
sources: John Lynch, Simón Bolívar: A Life (2006)
Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre

stops.name: Ayacucho, the pampa of Quinua, the last battle
stops.campa: On the high plain below Quinua, some 5,800 patriots face 9,300 royalists under the last Viceroy of Peru. Sucre speaks the sentence his soldiers will keep for two hundred years: that on today's effort hangs the fate of South America, and in a battle scarcely three hours long, the royal army of the Andes is destroyed. La Serna is wounded and captured; Canterac, commanding what remains, sends within the hour to treat for terms. The war begun on the Orinoco delta ends on this Peruvian pampa.
stops.quote: ¡Soldados! De los esfuerzos de hoy pende la suerte de la América del Sur; otro día de gloria va a coronar vuestra admirable constancia.
stops.quote_source: Sucre, address to the army before Ayacucho, 9 December 1824
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Ayacucho at the pampa of Quinua
The equestrian monument to the Mariscal de Ayacucho at Quinua

stops.name: Ayacucho, the gentleman's capitulation
stops.campa: By nightfall Sucre and Canterac sign eighteen articles that end three centuries of empire without a single vindictive clause: the defeated generals, chiefs and officers keep their uniforms and their swords, their servants remain with them, and no Spaniard who chooses to stay in America shall be persecuted for his politics or his past. It is remembered less for its terms than for its temper: a courtesy offered by the victor of a war that had, on both sides, forgotten courtesy years before.
stops.quote: Los generales, jefes y oficiales conservarán el uso de sus uniformes y espadas; y podrán tener consigo a su servicio los asistentes correspondientes a sus clases.
suggested_refs: The eighteen articles of the Capitulation of Ayacucho, 9 December 1824

stops.name: Lima, the courier, and the title of Gran Mariscal
stops.campa: The dispatch reaches Lima and Bolívar, waiting there under Congress's own recall, casts off his coat and cries the victory through the halls of La Magdalena, giving the glory wholly to the man he sent in his place. Within weeks the Peruvian Congress names Sucre Gran Mariscal de Ayacucho and the Colombian Congress raises him to general en jefe: the two republics he has just finished liberating competing to thank him first.
stops.quote: La batalla de Ayacucho es la cumbre de la gloria americana, y la obra del general Sucre.
stops.quote_source: Simón Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre (1825)
suggested_refs: The title 'Gran Mariscal de Ayacucho', conferred 12 February 1825
sources: Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre
bolivar.journey.json (Lima, the news of Ayacucho, shared moment)

segments.name: Alto Perú, the Founding of Bolivia

stops.name: La Paz, the decree that opens Upper Peru
stops.campa: Under Bolívar's orders Sucre crosses the Desaguadero into Upper Peru, the last royalist ground on the continent, and in La Paz on 9 February issues the decree that lets its people choose their own destiny: union with Peru, union with Buenos Aires, or a nation of their own. It is an unusual sentence for a soldier to write with his own hand: an army of liberation offering, instead of a flag, a ballot.
suggested_refs: The decree of La Paz, 9 February 1825, opening the question of Upper Peru's fate
sources: el-carabobeno.com, 'Alto Perú, República de Bolívar, 6 de agosto de 1825'

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the Assembly declares a nation and names it for the living
stops.campa: Sucre reconvenes the Assembly he has summoned at Chuquisaca, and on 6 August, chosen for the date of Junín, the battle he did not fight but built on, the delegates of Charcas, Potosí, La Paz, Cochabamba and Santa Cruz sign the Independence Act of the Departments of Upper Peru. Within days they resolve to call the new republic Bolivia, the only nation on earth ever named for a living man, and its liberator has, in effect, midwifed his own commander into godfather.
suggested_refs: The Casa de la Libertad, Chuquisaca (Sucre), hall of the 1825 declaration

stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosí, the flags on the silver summit
stops.campa: On 26 October Sucre climbs the Cerro Rico beside Bolívar, arrived at last from the north with the Argentine envoys Alvear and Díaz Vélez in train, and on the summit of the mountain that fed three centuries of Spanish treasuries the flags of Colombia, Peru and the young Argentine provinces are planted together. Bolívar speaks of the road from the Orinoco's mangroves to this peak of silver as the war's true completion; Sucre, who fought the last and hardest half of that road, stands beside him as the campaign's other half made visible.
stops.quote: Estando sobre esta masa de plata que se llama Potosí, cuyas venas riquísimas fueron trescientos años el erario de España, yo estimo en nada esta opulencia cuando la comparo con la gloria de haber traído el estandarte de la libertad victorioso desde las playas ardientes del Orinoco, para fijarlo aquí, en el pico de este monte.
stops.quote_source: Bolívar, speech on the summit of Cerro Rico de Potosí, 26 October 1825, spoken with Sucre present
suggested_refs: El Cerro Rico de Potosí
alvear.journey.json and bolivar.journey.json (Cerro Rico summit, shared pin)

stops.name: Chuquisaca, sworn in as the first President of Bolivia
stops.campa: Elected constitutional president on 26 May, Sucre takes his oath in Chuquisaca on the 28th, thirty-one years old and governing the nation he made. He writes for it, at Bolívar's dictation, a constitution with a lifetime presidency, the Liberator's strangest and most confessional law, tried nowhere but here, and calls the little republic his own creation with something between a soldier's pride and a father's. Nowhere in the whole war does the arc of the campaign rest as visibly as on this one signature.
suggested_refs: The Constitución Vitalicia of Bolivia, 1826
Casa de la Libertad, Sucre, seat of the first presidency

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the mutiny, the bullet, the ruined arm
stops.campa: Foreign officers and Peruvian intrigue, chiefly Casimiro Olañeta's, bring the garrison of Chuquisaca to mutiny before dawn. Sucre walks unguarded to the barracks of San Francisco to face the men down as he has faced worse all his life, and the answer he gets is a volley: a ball grazes his head, another shatters the bone of his right arm. He survives, but the arm never truly heals: the sword-hand of Pichincha and Ayacucho left useless for the eleven years he has left to live.
suggested_refs: The Motín de Chuquisaca, 18 April 1828
sources: abi.bo, '18 de abril de 1828, el primer golpe de Estado'

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the resignation, a nation asked to forgive nothing
stops.campa: Wounded, unable now to govern a country pulling itself apart between Lima and La Paz, Sucre resigns on 2 August and leaves Chuquisaca within days, his arm in a sling, a servant and one aide his whole escort. His farewell message asks the nation for a single reward beyond thanks, that Bolivia not be destroyed by those who inherit it, and he says of his own two years in power what almost no departing ruler of this age can honestly say: no widow, no orphan grieves on his account.
stops.quote: No he hecho gemir a ningún boliviano: ninguna viuda, ningún huérfano sollozan por mi causa... He señalado mi gobierno por la clemencia, la tolerancia y la bondad.
stops.quote_source: Sucre, farewell message to the Bolivian nation, 2 August 1828
suggested_refs: Sucre's farewell message to Bolivia, 2 August 1828
sources: Ley boliviana de 12 de agosto de 1828 (LexiVox)

segments.name: Quito, Marriage and the War of Tarqui

stops.name: Quito, married by proxy, two days after the mutiny
stops.campa: Six years to the season after a laurel crown fell from a Quito balcony onto another man's brow, the woman who threw it, Mariana Carcelén, Marquesa de Solanda, who has courted Sucre by letter through every campaign since Pichincha, marries him in Quito on 20 April. He is not there: still president of Bolivia, still two days bandaged from the shot that broke his arm at Chuquisaca, he stands at his own wedding by proxy, General Vicente Aguirre wearing his absence at the altar.
suggested_refs: Mariana Carcelén, Marquesa de Solanda, and the Carcelén Mansion in Quito

stops.name: Quito, the Carcelén mansion, a life finally begun
stops.campa: Released at last from Bolivia and from the presidency, Sucre rides north to Quito and, on 30 September, walks for the first time into the house of the wife he married without meeting. Mariana Carcelén becomes, for the little time left to them, mistress of a household instead of a correspondence; a daughter, Teresa, will be born to them within the year. The soldier who has not stopped moving since he was fifteen tries, for a season, to stop.
suggested_refs: The Carcelén Mansion, Quito, home of the Marquesa de Solanda
sources: vistazo.com, 'La historia oculta de la vida y muerte del mariscal Antonio José de Sucre'

stops.name: Portete de Tarqui, the last battle fought for Gran Colombia
stops.campa: Peru, under La Mar and Gamarra, invades Gran Colombia's south over the old quarrel of Guayaquil; called from his brief peace, Sucre takes the field once more at the narrow pass of the Portete de Tarqui above Girón, where a ravine lets men cross only shoulder to shoulder. The Peruvian vanguard is destroyed there on 27 February; Colombian cavalry, badly mauled in the counter-charge, cannot press the advantage further, but the invasion is broken and the frontier holds. It is his last battle, fought one-armed, thirty-four years old.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of the Portete de Tarqui, near Girón, Azuay

stops.name: Girón, the armistice that ends the war of brothers
stops.campa: Sucre and La Mar treat at Girón for the peace that Tarqui's stalemate has forced on both sides; the Armistice of Piura, signed in July, restores Guayaquil to Colombia, returns the frontier to what it was before the invasion, and ends the strange, sad war between the two republics that Ayacucho's own victor and the government he helped seat in Lima had, five years before, liberated together.
suggested_refs: The Armistice of Piura, 10 July 1829, ending the Gran Colombia-Peru War

segments.name: Bogotá and Berruecos, the Congress and the Ambush

stops.name: Bogotá, president of the Congreso Admirable
stops.campa: Bolívar convenes in Bogotá, on 20 January, the congress that history will call Admirable: the last attempt to hold Gran Colombia together against the pull of Venezuela, New Granada, and Ecuador toward separate lives. The delegates elect Sucre its president, the soldier who liberated four countries now asked to chair the funeral of the fifth idea, the union itself. He accepts, presides with the same patience he brought to the capitulation of Ayacucho, and cannot save what the delegates have already, in their hearts, let go.
suggested_refs: The Congreso Admirable, Bogotá, January-May 1830
sources: Wikipedia, 'Asesinato de Antonio José de Sucre'

stops.name: Bogotá, the road south, against every warning
stops.campa: With Bolívar's own resignation accepted and the congress dissolved, Sucre sets out for Quito to rejoin Mariana and the daughter he has barely met, riding south by the Pan-American road through Popayán toward Pasto: country he knows to be hostile, where the caudillo José María Obando holds the province by force and grievance and has reason, political and personal, to fear the arriving Mariscal. Friends urge another route, a larger escort; he declines both, the same habit of unguarded courage that walked him into the mutineers' fire at Chuquisaca two years before.
suggested_refs: The road from Bogotá to Quito via Popayán and Pasto, 1830
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Asesinato de Antonio José de Sucre'
elcomercio.com, 'El asesinato de Sucre en Berruecos'

stops.name: Popayán, the last calm crossing
stops.campa: He passes through Popayán at the end of May, resting briefly among acquaintances who will later testify to how plainly he traveled: a small party, little baggage, nothing of the pomp his rank could have claimed. From here the road climbs into the mountains toward Pasto, through the district Obando governs and the pass called Berruecos, a place already ill-famed in the province for ambush. Sucre rides on into it anyway, thirteen leagues short of Pasto.
suggested_refs: Popayán, last city before the pass of Berruecos
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Asesinato de Antonio José de Sucre'

stops.name: Berruecos, the forest road, four shots, thirty-five years old
stops.campa: On the mountain trail between El Cabuyal and La Jacoba, in the forest called Berruecos, gunmen hired by Colonel Apolinar Morillo and José Erazo, the plot laid, the record shows, at Obando's own instance, fire on Sucre from the trees. Four balls strike him: head, neck, breast. He falls from his mule and dies on the forest path, thirty-five years old, four months and six days before the man he served will die of his own broken health at Santa Marta, calling the murder of Sucre the day something in him could not survive.
stops.quote: ¡Santo Dios! ¡Se ha derramado la sangre de Abel! ... La bala cruel que le hirió el corazón, mató a Colombia y me quitó la vida.
stops.quote_source: Bolívar, on hearing of Sucre's assassination, Cartagena, 1 July 1830 (accounts of his aides; O'Leary, Memorias)
suggested_refs: The monument to Antonio José de Sucre at Berruecos, Arboleda, Nariño
